segments.heading: Myth

segments.heading: Math 1
segments.narration: A $1,200 TV on a store card: 'no interest if paid in full in 12 months.' That's deferred interest.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a TV with a small tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 2
segments.narration: You pay $90 a month. After 12 months, $1,080 is paid and $120 is left.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin stack with a small gap. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 3
segments.narration: Interest at an example 26.99% is charged back to day one on the whole $1,200: roughly $175.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar flipping back. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Verdict
segments.narration: It's free only if you clear every dollar in time. Miss by $120, pay about $175.
segments.on_screen_text: Free only if paid in FULL
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a balance scale tipping. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rule
segments.narration: Divide the price by 11, not 12, and pay that. $1,200 ÷ 11 ≈ $110 a month.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small card with a check mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.caption:
Deferred interest ("no interest if paid in full") isn't the same as 0% APR. Leave $120 unpaid and interest can be charged on the full purchase back to day one: about $175 in this example at 26.99%.

Pay price ÷ 11 each month to finish early.

segments.narration: The myth: a raise can push you into a higher bracket and cut your pay. Let's check it with arithmetic.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a speech bubble with a question mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 1
segments.narration: Example brackets (simplified): 12% up to $50,000 of taxable income, 22% above it.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a two-step staircase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 2
segments.narration: A raise takes taxable income from $49,000 to $52,000. Only $2,000 lands on the 22% step.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin on the top step. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 3
segments.narration: Extra federal income tax: $120 + $440 = $560. You keep about $2,440 of the $3,000 raise before payroll and state tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin stack with a small slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Verdict
segments.narration: Only the dollars above each line are taxed at the higher rate. A raise always means more after income tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a balance scale tipping. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rule
segments.narration: Take the raise. Then raise your savings rate with part of it.
segments.on_screen_text: Take it · save part of it
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small card with a check mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.caption:
Brackets are a staircase: only income above each line is taxed at the higher rate. In this simplified example, a $3,000 raise adds $560 of federal income tax ($1,000 × 12% + $2,000 × 22%). You keep about $2,440 before payroll and state tax. Check IRS.gov for current brackets.

Educational, not tax or financial advice. Check IRS.gov for your situation.

segments.heading: Myth

segments.on_screen_text: MYTH: Rent vs own: real costs
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a speech bubble with a question mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 1
segments.narration: Owning a $350,000 home with 20% down: a $280,000 loan at an example 6.5%.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a house with a key. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 2
segments.narration: First-year costs you never get back: about $1,517/mo interest, $350 tax, $150 insurance, $292 maintenance.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. four small coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Math 3
segments.narration: Compare: rent for a similar place, an example $1,800 a month, plus about $15 renters insurance.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. an apartment with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Verdict
segments.narration: Owners 'throw away' money too: interest, taxes, insurance and repairs. It depends on prices and how long you stay.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a balance scale tipping. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rule
segments.narration: Compare unrecoverable costs, not rent vs mortgage. Plan to stay 5+ years before buying.

script.caption:
Rent vs own (example): $350K home, $280K at 6.5%. First-year unrecoverable costs ≈ $1,517/mo interest + $350 property tax + $150 insurance + $292 maintenance (1%/yr) ≈ $2,309/mo, vs ~$1,815 rent + renters insurance. Owning builds equity and may appreciate; renting keeps the down payment free to invest. It depends on prices and time.
